Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Hay-Zama Wood Bison Aerial Survey (2025) 
Background 
The Hay-Zama wood bison population (Bison bison 
athabascae) was established through the introduction 
of wood bison to the area. This was part of a national 
effort to recover wood bison populations and the 
establish free ranging, self-sustaining and disease-free 
wood bison in each of the provinces and territories in 
Western Canada. The Hay-Zama population has 
historically been managed by a regulated hunting 
season to maintain a population objective between 
400 and 600 animals. This objective accomplishes a 
sustainable population while also limiting distribution 
toward diseased bison to the east, in and adjacent to 
Wood Buffalo National Park and helping reduce 
conflicts in communities and roadways. A minimum 
total count is conducted annually in late February or 
March. All bison found are counted and classified as 
adult or calf to determine the herd composition. 
Survey Method 
The 2025 Hay-Zama bison survey was conducted by 
flying transects orientated east-west and spaced one 
degree of latitude apart (roughly one statue mile) 
within an expanded search area, encompassing the 
historical range. The search area was expanded 
slightly to the North and to the south to cover areas of 
expected bison occupancy. A fixed-wing aircraft was 
also deployed to fly the range periphery to track and/or 
locate any potential bison occurrence beyond the 
traditional survey area to ensure all bison groups were 
observed. The crew consisted of 3 observers in each 
of two Bell 206 Jet Rangers equipped with bubble 
windows in the rear. Survey speed was approximately 
90 to 110 km per hour. All groups were photographed 
to confirm total counts and classification of adults and 
calves. The adult classification includes juveniles and 
both sexes due to the difficulty in accurately separating 
between sex and age classes. Calves were classified 
based on relative size and shorter nasal bridge. 
Results and Discussion 
The Hay-Zama bison survey was undertaken from 
February 25-28, 2025. A total of 678 bison (511 adults 
and 167 calves) were seen in 51 groups. There were 
25 percent calves which is higher than the previous 5-
year average (17%).
